notes: Toll-Knight; born Toren Tamwick; the day watch at the Choir; the bottle of vinegar a year from his sister and no letter. The Order as the Bell account lived by somebody from the Candle's valley.

greetings.text: You have been to Tamwick. Is the press turning? Do not tell me anything else. The press turning is all I have asked about in seventeen years and I will not start now.
Vigil. You have taken the grey and the count. Then you know what the Seat is holding, or you will, and I am sorry for you, and glad.

It is decided, whatever you decided. Cadwen says the count changed the night you came out of the Seat. I did not count that night. I stood at the ring and did not count, for the first time in seventeen years, and it was very quiet.
The Order counts bells. It does not count what a pilgrim did before the grey. Stand where I can see you all the same.
Stand off the yard while the forms are going. The clapper is bound, but a bound bell-mace will still take a shoulder out.

greet.speaker: Toren Ash
greet.text: Ash. Toll-Knight. Every knight of the Order is Ash; the name comes with the vigil, and what we were before is written once, inside the bell, where you have to lie down to read it. I keep the day watch at the Choir. Cadwen keeps the night. Between us the ring is never unwatched.

hub.speaker: Toren Ash
hub.text: Speak softly. Everything here is heard.

choices.text: What is the Tolling Order's vigil?
Who were you before the grey?
Why does your clapper smell of apples?
What is the Sunken Choir?
What does the Dwindling look like from the ring?
I'll leave you to the watch.

the_vigil.speaker: Toren Ash
the_vigil.text: Twelve headless colossi in a ring round the Cantor's Seat, and inside the Seat a note that has not stopped for a thousand years, and the Order stands at the ring and counts bells. That is all. Day and night, both watches, since the ones who turned back from the Hush in the Ash Winter founded it. — The Sayers read the last two words on the Toll's crown as a signature. We read them as a report: the holder holds. Present tense. Still true. Somebody has to stand at the door of a thing like that and count what comes out of it, and it is us, and we are grim and kind and we know how it ends.

before.speaker: Toren Ash
before.text: Toren Tamwick. The press. My sister Bessa keeps the orchards and my brother Hob turns the screw and I was the one who could not stay in a valley where every window is lit on Candle Night and nobody asks what the light is for. — I walked south at twenty-seven to find out. I found the Order at the ring counting, and Cadwen, two years sworn and already the one the rest looked to, handed me a clapper-cloth and did not ask my name, and I have not said it aloud since, except to you, now, and I do not know why I did.

vinegar.speaker: Toren Ash
vinegar.text: A bottle a year from Tamwick. Cider vinegar, no letter. Seventeen bottles. — Bessa does not write. She grafts. The bottle is the letter: it says the press is turning and the trees are alive and she has not forgiven me and she has not stopped. I polish the clapper-cloth with it, and for a week each spring the vigil at the Choir smells of the Vale, and Cadwen pretends not to notice, and Deseith turns to face the smell as if it were a bell. — I have never written back. In the Vale a loaf carried to a door is a sentence and three is a friendship. A bottle a year is exactly what I have earned, and I know it, and I would not have it be more.

the_choir.speaker: Toren Ash
the_choir.text: Twelve statues fifty metres tall in a ring, and not one of them has a head. They lost them in one night, before the Toll fell, and the Oroth began to go out of the record that same year. From the Mere they look like a crown of stumps. From the ring they look like people who have turned away. — Stand at the ring at noon and you will hear a bell every few minutes, from nowhere, and under it a note, always, from the Seat. We count the bells. Twelve to the day, always twelve, since the Order began. On Skerrday Deseith counted eleven, and Cadwen made him count again, aloud, with her, and it was eleven. She has not said what she thinks. I have not asked. I am the day watch; I count by day; the day count was twelve, and I am holding to it.

dwindling.speaker: Toren Ash
dwindling.text: The Order does not have an account. It has a door. — The Bell says the world is a note struck once and fading, and the Seat holds the wrong note, and the dead in the deep places are held in it. I was raised on the Candle: tend your hearth and say your neighbour's name and the flame stays lit. I have stood seventeen years at a ring where nobody's name is said and the note has never once gone out, and I have had to make my peace with the fact that the valley I love is wrong about the largest thing in the world. — So I count. It is not an account. It is what you do at a door when you do not know what is on the other side and you have decided not to leave.

bye.speaker: Toren Ash
bye.text: Go softly on the ash. Not for the wights; they wave. For the note. It hears feet, and I would rather it went on hearing ours.

notes: Sutler to the pilgrims; a Larkbourne Ford thatcher in grey with a purse under it. Two tallies on the cart lid: bells inside, marks outside. Sells through the trade choice.

greetings.text: Cart's open. Grey cloth, ash-cake, candles. Everything a person needs to give up everything. Speak soft; they get upset if you haggle loud.
You have coin on you. I can hear it. Do not let it clink in the yard; Cadwen will look at you the way she looks at me, and I have had nine years of that look and I do not recommend it.
I sell to anybody. That is not virtue; a sutler with principles is a sutler with an empty cart. But I will count the bells while you are here, out loud, and you can decide what that is.
You know Merrowby. Then you know the market; I am there Hushdays with my hood down, and if you saw a grey man buying candles by the gross and pretending to be somebody else, that was me pretending.
The bells are ahead of the marks by six. It was a slow week for both. You may buy; the lid says so.

greet.speaker: Wat Thatcher
greet.text: Thatcher. Wat. I was a thatcher, at Larkbourne Ford, two cottages and a bridge, and I came here to put on grey and count bells like everyone, and I found a camp of people who had given up everything and had nobody to sell them a candle. So. The grey is real. So is the purse. I have stopped pretending either one away.

hub.speaker: Wat Thatcher
hub.text: What can I do for you, softly?

choices.text: Why does a pilgrim need a sutler?
What are the scratches on your cart lid?
Why did you come south?
Somebody found the red poppy?
What is the Dwindling to a man with a purse?
That's all.

the_trade.speaker: Wat Thatcher
the_trade.text: Because giving up everything takes candles. And grey cloth, which does not grow on the heath, and ash-cake, which nobody in the Vale would eat and which is what there is. The Order feeds the mad and the knights; the rest of us walk here from every corner of the basin with what we are wearing and a bell in our heads, and by the second week we want a hood that does not leak. — I bring it up from Merrowby on Hushdays with the cart. They pay what they have. Some have a lot; you would be surprised who walks south. I take it. I take less than the Row would. Cadwen says that is not the same as taking none and she is right and I take it anyway.

the_tallies.speaker: Wat Thatcher
the_tallies.text: Inside the lid, every bell I have heard since I came. Outside, every mark I have taken. — The bells are always ahead. I keep them ahead. When the marks get within a hand of the bells I shut the cart and sit in the yard with the pilgrims and count until the Choir has rung enough that I can open it again in good conscience, or what I have instead of one. Nine years. The bells are ahead by six this week. That is my whole religion and it fits on a lid, and Deseith says it is the most honest count in the camp because it is the only one that costs the counter anything.

why_south.speaker: Wat Thatcher
why_south.text: The Ford went quiet. Not quiet the way the Roll means; there are still two cottages and a bridge and the Boys on the road. Quiet the way a house is when the child has grown and gone and you keep hearing her on the stair. I had thatched every roof between Merrowby and the Rest and one morning I stood on a ridge with the reed in my hands and could not think what a roof was for. — So I walked south to find out what was under everything, like a fool, and found a camp that needed candles. It is not what I came for. It is what there was. A thatcher knows about working with what there is.

the_poppy.speaker: Wat Thatcher
the_poppy.text: West of the Choir, on Skerrday. A pilgrim woman, three weeks in the grey, found the red one. There is one to a square kilometre of this heath and most people go a year without; I have been here nine and seen two. I offered her forty marks on the spot. I would have got two hundred for it at the Row. — She looked at me. Then she ate it, petals and all, standing there, and said it tasted of nothing, and that was the point, and walked back to the tents. I scratched a bell on the inside of the lid for that. It was not a bell. It should have been.

dwindling.speaker: Wat Thatcher
dwindling.text: Everything here costs a little more and is worth a little less, every year, and I am the only man in Cinderlea who has the figures. Candles that burned a night burn most of one. Grey cloth that was grey is greyer. Ash-cake that was bad is the same, which is the one thing that holds. — The Sayers have four accounts. I have a ledger, and the ledger says the world is being marked down, and I do not know by whom, and I keep the bells ahead of the marks because it is the only thing on the lid I can still make go the right way.

bye.speaker: Wat Thatcher
bye.text: Mind the ash-cake; it is better than it looks and worse than it tastes. Come back Hushday if you want Merrowby bread; I bring a loaf up for Aud Fennick and she will not eat it, so.

notes: A pilgrim who gave his name away; the Tollmere clerk who heard the note through the floor. Faces the last bell. Speaks softly, counts, and is exact about what he does not know.

greetings.text: Eleven. — Forgive me. I was at eleven. It is usually twelve by now. Speak softly; the twelfth may still come.
You have been in the city. Did you hear it through the floor? No. Nobody does. Only me, once, and I have not been able to stop, and I do not want to.
I face the bells. I do not face people. So I cannot say what you are, and I would rather not, and that is a kindness on both sides.
It changed. The note. The night you were inside. I turned to face it and it was not where it had been, and I have been facing the new place since, and nobody has told me if that is right.
You know what I was called. Please do not say it. I will not turn to it, and it will hurt us both to find that out.

greet.speaker: Deseith
greet.text: Deseith. That is the name I took. I heard it in the note, or I heard the note and the name was the shape my mouth made; I have never been sure and the Order says it does not matter. Speak softly. I will face you while there is no bell, and when there is, I will turn, and you must not mind.

choices.text: Why do you face the bells?
What did you hear in Tollmere?
What was your name?
You counted eleven?
What is the Dwindling, to you?
I'll let you listen.

facing.speaker: Deseith
facing.text: Because a bell is a direction. Everyone here counts them; Cadwen counts them, the sutler counts them on his lid. I count them and I turn. Whatever is ringing out there is somewhere, and if I face it, then for the time until the next one I am pointed at the thing that is happening, and not at the ash. — The pilgrims tell the time by me. Deseith is facing the Choir; it is past noon. Deseith is facing the Hush; something rang in the south and nobody else heard it. That last one happens. Not often. I do not tell Cadwen. She would want to go and look.

the_floor.speaker: Deseith
the_floor.text: I kept a ledger in a counting-house on Lantern Row. Wharfage and fines, in a fair hand. One Thornday I was totalling a column and I heard a note come up through the floor, through the Oroth stone the whole island is built on, one note, low, held, from the south. I put down the pen. Nobody else in the room had heard anything. — I have heard it every moment since. Through floors, through my own sleep, through the sound of the sutler haggling. I walked south because if you can hear a thing from a hundred miles away, you should at least go and stand near it and find out whether it is a thing or whether it is you. It is a thing. That was a comfort for about a day.

old_name.speaker: Deseith
old_name.text: I gave it at the bell yard. You say it once to Cadwen and she does not write it down and you do not say it again. — Something the Sayers do to people they want gone, they call it unsaying, and it is done with malice and takes a century. I did it to myself in an afternoon with a knight watching, kindly, and it took. There is a man's name in Orrin Quill's day-book at the Row against a column of wharfage, and it is not mine any more, and if you said it aloud in this yard I would not turn to it. I have tested that. I asked Aud Fennick to say it once, and she did, softly, and I went on facing the Choir, and she wept, and I could not think why.

eleven.speaker: Deseith
eleven.text: On Skerrday. Between noon and dusk, twelve bells, always; the Order has counted twelve since the Ash Winter. I counted eleven and turned eleven times and stood facing the eleventh waiting for the twelfth, and it did not come, and it was dark. — Cadwen made me count again with her, aloud, the next day. Eleven. She said nothing. Toren counts by day and says his count was twelve, and I believe him, and I believe me, and one of the Choir's bells has stopped ringing for the man who faces it and not for the man who does not, and I do not know what that means and I have decided it means it is my bell that stopped.

dwindling.speaker: Deseith
dwindling.text: I heard the world's note through a floor and I have been facing it for nine years, and what I can tell you is that it is a little further away each year. Not quieter. Further. As if the thing making it were walking backwards, slowly, and I am turning to follow, and one day I will have turned all the way round and be facing the Hush, and that will be where it has gone. — The Order says the holder holds. I say the holder is holding and walking backwards at the same time, and nobody has ever told them you cannot do both.

bye.speaker: Deseith
bye.text: Go softly. If you hear a bell as you go, tell me which way it was. I will have turned to it, but it is good to be told I was right.

notes: The one who lays Greyfold's tables. Forty-one places, the forty-second on Hushday, the wights that wave, the letter under the plate at the third house (core:book/letter_from_greyfold). She will not leave, and it is not grief.

greetings.text: They are coming to stand. Do not step between a place and the one it is laid for; they are polite, and you would not be.
Wait until the places are laid. Forty-one. Forty-two. Then you may sit at the foot, where nobody is.

You have read the letter. Then you know it was for her sister at Gullhithe, by any hand going north. There was none. There is still none. I am not a hand going north; I am the hand that puts the plate back.
You may sit. Everyone may sit. They sat down to a meal and stood up into the ash and nobody at this table has ever asked anyone what they had done.
That is one of my spoons. Put it back at the place you took it from. I know which. So do they.

greet.speaker: Nan Greyfold
greet.text: Greyfold. I took the name; nobody else was going to. I lay the tables. Forty-one places, every dawn, cleared every dusk, wiped of ash. They come and stand at them in the evening and wave, and I wave back, and then I go in and shut the door. That is Greyfold. You may sit at the foot.

hub.speaker: Nan Greyfold
hub.text: Ask, if you like. I have not had anyone to ask me in a while.

choices.text: Why lay tables for the dead?
What happened here?
The forty-second place?
You found the letter?
What does the Dwindling look like from this table?
I'll leave you the lane.

the_tables.speaker: Nan Greyfold
the_tables.text: They were laid when I came. Thirty-one years ago; I was a pilgrim, three weeks in the grey, walking to the Choir like everyone, and I came down this lane and the tables were laid for a meal nobody finished, and the ash on the plates was an inch deep, and I sat down. — I do not know why. I have had thirty-one years to think of a reason and the honest one is that the places were set and nobody was sitting in them, and I was raised in the Vale, where a laid place with nobody in it is a thing you cannot walk past. So I wiped a spoon. Then another. They came at dusk and stood at their places and waved. I have laid the tables every morning since, and the Order sends bread, and I am not sad, whatever Cadwen thinks. I am occupied.

ash_winter.speaker: Nan Greyfold
ash_winter.text: Cinderlea burned for a year, in eight sixty-six. The ash stopped one morning and the people of Greyfold went out and looked, and it was grey, all of it, the heath and the sky and the line between, and they sat down to a meal, and they stood up from it and walked south into the Hush, singing. All of them. The ones who turned back at the edge founded the Order. — Nobody knows why they walked. The letter under the plate says they had grain. They were not starving and they were not mad. I think they were tidy people, and they had seen that the world was going, and they went out to meet it rather than have it come in through the door with its boots on. That is a Vale thought and I am a Vale woman, and I lay the tables because they should have finished their meal first.

forty_second.speaker: Nan Greyfold
forty_second.text: Forty-one places, for forty-one who stood up. On Hushday I laid forty-two. — I will not say for whom. I will say that they all came and stood round it at dusk, every one of them, and waved at it, and it was empty, and they have never once in thirty-one years waved at an empty place. So it is not empty. I do not know who it is for. Something in the lane knows. I am seventy and I lay a place every morning for whoever is coming, and I think for the first time in thirty-one years that somebody is.

the_letter.speaker: Nan Greyfold
the_letter.text: Under a plate at the third house, which is mine now. 'To my sister at Gullhithe, by any hand going north.' Folded and not carried. — I read it once. I put it back under the plate. A man from the Spire came through with a satchel and copied it out and took the copy north and it is a book now, they tell me, that people buy. The letter is still under the plate. It was addressed and it was not carried, and I am not a hand going north; I am the hand that puts the plate back. If her sister's line at Gullhithe is still there — Wicks, I think; there are Wicks there still — then it is theirs to come south for, and they have not, and I lay a place for the woman who wrote it every morning, seventh from the head on the left, and she stands at it.

dwindling.speaker: Nan Greyfold
dwindling.text: I lay forty-one places and forty-one come. That is my account. — The Vale says a person nobody speaks of goes quiet and one day is not there. The people of Greyfold have been spoken of by nobody for a hundred and seventy-seven years except me, and I do not speak of them; I lay their places. And they are there. Every dusk. Waving. So either the Candle is wrong, or laying a place is a kind of speaking, and I have decided it is the second, and I have decided that a spoon wiped of ash is a name said, and I have said forty-one names a day for thirty-one years with a cloth, and that is more tending than the whole of Merrowby has done for anybody, and I would like that written down somewhere, and I know it will not be.

bye.speaker: Nan Greyfold
bye.text: Go up the lane, not across the tables. And if you pass the seventh place on the left, do not look at it too long. She is shy. She was shy in the letter too.
